segments.narration: OMAR: Welcome to RCM Part A: Documentation & Coding. You will practise decisions that help you act with confidence. You will leave with practical actions for your next shift.
segments.on_screen_text: "Documentation & coding that gets approved" · "RCM Part A"
segments.speaker: omar

segments.narration: OMAR: The reviewer only has your note. Good documentation protects the patient, you and the clinic. Keep the main point connected to a familiar task or conversation. That connection makes the information easier to use when it matters. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision.
segments.on_screen_text: "The payer doesn't see your patient. The payer sees your note." · Clinical decision + documentation + coding = optimised payment
segments.speaker: omar

segments.narration: OMAR: This reflection is not scored. Choose the response that helps you set one intention for your next shift.

segments.narration: OMAR: What always goes in, what never should. Use the tabs as a short reference, not a checklist to race through. Notice which detail would guide your next conversation or decision. Ask early when a situation does not match the rule. Good habits here are quiet: check, confirm, continue. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task.
segments.on_screen_text: Always: chief complaint & HPI · relevant findings · link symptoms to the working diagnosis · labs/imaging when needed · Avoid: vague notes · diagnosis without support · copy-paste · "fatigue only", "body pain"
segments.speaker: omar

segments.narration: NOOR: Same patient, same fluids. One note gets paid. Use the comparison to separate a helpful detail from a potential problem. The important step is turning what you see into a clear response. Good habits here are quiet: check, confirm, continue. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear.
segments.on_screen_text: Before: "Patient given IV fluids." · After: "Dehydration signs (HR 112, dry mucosa) — IV fluids started for stabilisation." Rendered as two note cards (SVG)

segments.narration: OMAR: Coding is clinical translation. Specific codes get accepted. Notice which part of the information you would need first in practice. segments.narration: OMAR: Talk through the provisional diagnosis: honest about uncertainty, still specific. Follow the example one step at a time, then identify why the next step makes sense. segments.on_screen_text: Fever 3 days + dysuria + suprapubic pain → urinalysis and culture ordered → document a provisional diagnosis linked to the findings → confirm or change when results return. Self-explanation: "Why is a provisional diagnosis better than 'fever' here?"

segments.narration: OMAR: Defensive medicine feels safe but gets rejected. Follow work-up protocols, document deviations. As you read, focus on the decision this information supports in your own role. The aim is a practical next action, not a phrase to memorise. Notice which part of this you would use first on shift. The aim is a decision you can repeat, not a phrase to recall. Link it to the task waiting for you tomorrow. If one detail stays with you, let it be the safe one.
segments.on_screen_text: Follow initial work-up protocols · No supplements without indication · Repeat only at evidence-based intervals · If you deviate, document why
segments.speaker: omar
